metadata.color_semantics: Claude FIDELITY skin: cream #F2F0E9 stage, warm ink #3D3929, terracotta #D97757 as the ONE accent — one terracotta moment per beat. The source Mycroft figures used crimson #C8102E for the data series and ochre #C8860E for annotation; both remap onto the Claude accent grammar (terracotta = data series and single focal moment, ink = structure, muted ink = de-emphasis). Palette change only, no data change. Same treatment as week 1.
metadata.derived_from: narration_script.md (human-authored, 438 spoken words, target 2:55). Every on-screen figure is drawn from figdata_week2.json, which the Mycroft repo queries directly from the built Parquet — no number is typed by hand, so a chart cannot drift from the panel it describes.
metadata.note: ai-explainer / claude-hai. ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00 (cold open, answered), B08 (verdict artifact), B09 (handoff) and B10 (outro) only — every body beat illustrates its concept as a native animated Remotion scene (REBUILD LAW). The three source PNGs in pantry/ are REFERENCE for the rebuild, never slotted as media; their SVG sources travel with them. The script pairs two traps in one shot and puts the staircase and the archive-lag problem on one figure; both are split here so each beat carries one idea.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. Week two of the Private AI Valuation Agent. Last week I proved by hand that S E C filings give you a share price for companies that have no public price. This week I scaled that from one company to fourteen quarters of data, and the machine immediately found three things my hand check had missed.

show.event: Cream Claude composer, empty. Serif greeting 'Hej, HAI' + terracotta spark above it.
The ask types itself into the composer, character by character.
Send button arms terracotta; running indicator reads 'ingesting 14 quarters…'.
Three output lines land in sequence — the ask arrives ANSWERED (COLD OPEN LAW).

props.command: Last week I verified one private company's share price by hand. Now scale it — fourteen quarters of SEC bulk data, every fund, every holding. What does the machine see that I couldn't?
output: a 33-point Anthropic price history, rebuilt from filings
three defects a hand-check was too small to see

beats.narration_text: Last week: one company, checked by hand. This week: eighty million rows, checked by machine. Scale does two things. It shows you the shape a private valuation actually moves in. And it finds the mistakes a hand check was too small to catch.

shot.visual_intent: The BLUF as kinetic type — what scale changes, stated before any specific. No data exhibit (EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW).

show.event: Left card sets: 'ONE COMPANY · by hand' with a small ink dot.
Right card sets much larger: '80,571,213 ROWS · by machine', terracotta.
A rule draws between them and two numbered outcomes stack beneath.
Outcome 1 types in: 'the SHAPE a private valuation moves in'.
Outcome 2 types in: 'the MISTAKES a hand-check was too small to catch'.

props.sparkLine: Scale changes what you can see.

beats.narration_text: I pulled fourteen quarters of the S E C's bulk data. About six gigabytes. Eighty and a half million individual holdings, every position held by every registered fund in the country. That filters down to twenty-two million private positions, and then to about fifty-eight hundred marks on the companies I track. Every stage reconciles against the stage above it.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w2-funnel.png. Three log-scaled stages; the collapse from stage two to stage three is the move that carries the beat (the script's own note).

show.event: Header sets; a '14 QUARTERS · 2023Q1–2026Q2 · ~5.9 GB' chip lands top-right.
Stage 1 bar draws full width in ink; counter races to 80,571,213.
An arrow drops and stage 2 draws shorter; counter races to 22,041,937.
Stage 3 COLLAPSES to a small terracotta block; counter lands on 5,806 — the drop is the point of the beat.
A tick appears beside each arrow and the footer sets: 'the last stage is 0.0072% of the first — every count reconciles to the row above'.

beats.narration_text: Here is what that buys. A price history for Anthropic, rebuilt entirely from filings. Thirty-three observation dates, from about twelve dollars a share in twenty twenty-three to over three hundred this April. Look at the shape. It is a staircase. The price sits flat for months, then jumps, because these marks only move when there is a new funding round.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w2-anthropic-staircase.png. The step line DRAWS left to right across the beat so the flat-then-jump shape is enacted, not described. All 33 points are the real medians from figdata_week2.json.

show.event: Axes draw; $0/$200/$400 gridlines and year ticks 2023–2026.
The step line begins drawing from the left at ~$12, one observation at a time.
The line has reached 2025; the flats visibly hold and the risers snap.
Every flat run highlights briefly in terracotta — the tread of each step reads as a held price.
The line completes to $333.60 and a caption sets: 'flat for months, then a step — marks move only on a repricing'.

props.title: Anthropic, priced by the funds that own it
props.subtitle: 33 period ends rebuilt from filings — marks move in steps, not drifts
props.caption: Flat for months, then a step — a mark only moves when a funding round reprices it.

beats.narration_text: And at that two fifty-nine step, seven completely independent fund managers. BlackRock, Fidelity, T. Rowe Price, Capital Group, and three more. All reporting the identical price, to the cent, on the same date. Twenty-four separate registrations, but only seven actual decision makers. Seven is the honest number.

shot.visual_intent: The convergence at $259.14, counted by FAMILY not by registration — the correction the figure layer nearly got wrong. Seven named managers converge on one number.

show.event: Seven name plates fan in around the frame, one per spoken/named manager.

show.at: on 'the identical price, to the cent'
show.event: A connector draws from each plate to the centre and $259.14 sets huge in terracotta.
24 small registration ticks appear beneath, then visibly GROUP into 7 clusters.
The count resolves to '24 registrations → 7 decision-makers' and the 7 holds.

props.title: Seven independent managers, one price, one date
props.caption: Counting registrations would have overstated independence — the exact error the family mapping exists to prevent.

beats.narration_text: Then I went looking for something and could not find it. The five eighty-nine mark I verified by hand last week is not in this data at all. The bulk archive is organized by when a fund files, not by the period the filing covers. Funds file about eight weeks late. So the newest data in the second quarter archive only reaches April thirtieth.

shot.visual_intent: The lag MECHANISM, not just the missing point: a period-end date and its filing date separated by ~56 days, which is why the 2026Q2 archive stops at 30 Apr and the $589 mark sits outside it.

show.event: A hollow terracotta circle labelled '$589.01 — verified by hand, week 1' sits alone at the right, outside a dashed boundary.

show.at: on 'organized by when a fund files'
show.event: Two parallel timelines appear: PERIOD COVERED above, FILED above it offset right.
A brace spans the offset and labels itself '~56 days'.
The archive boundary slides left to 30 Apr 2026 and the dashed line locks; the hollow circle stays visibly beyond it.
Caption: 'the archive is two months further behind than its own label suggests'.

props.sparkLine: Two months behind its own label.
props.title: The archive is keyed to when a fund files, not what it covers
props.missingSub: verified by hand in week 1 — not in the bulk data at all
props.caption: The whole archive sits two months further behind than its own label suggests. That single fact reshapes next week's work.

beats.narration_text: Two more traps, both caught before they did damage. Four of Fidelity's funds file under a name that never says Fidelity. Variable Insurance Products, one through four. My code counted one manager as five, inflating the exact number this project exists to measure.

shot.visual_intent: Five apparently-independent registrants visibly collapse into one manager — the inverse move of B04, and the reason B04's number is seven.

show.event: Five separate registrant cards stand apart, each with its CIK; four are named 'Variable Insurance Products Fund I–IV'.

show.at: on 'a name that never says Fidelity'
show.event: The word 'Fidelity' highlights terracotta in the one card that has it, and is conspicuously absent from the other four.
A counter reads 'independent managers: 5' in terracotta.
The five cards slide together into a single 'Fidelity' block and the counter drops 5 → 1.

props.title: Four funds that never say "Fidelity"
props.caption: Unmapped, they inflate precisely the count that cross-manager independence depends on.

beats.narration_text: And this. One SpaceX filing, one company. Common stock at a hundred and twelve dollars, and preferred at eleven twenty. Exactly ten times apart, inside a single document. Three hundred and nine cases of it across the panel, and no other company in the data does it at all.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w2-spacex-trap.png. The six real rows of one filing; the price column is where the beat lands, so the two bands separate on the spoken contrast.

show.event: The filing header sets and six rows land in sequence, numeric columns right-aligned to fixed rules.
The two EC rows' price cells set in ink at $112.00.
The four EP rows' price cells set terracotta at $1,120.00.
A brace joins the two price bands and '× 10' sets between them.
Footer sets: '309 of 624 SpaceX fund-periods — and no other company in the panel does it at all'.

props.title: One filing, one company, two prices exactly 10x apart

beats.narration_text: Week two on one page. Fourteen quarters loaded, eighty and a half million rows reconciled down to fifty-eight hundred marks. Anthropic's price history is a staircase, and seven independent managers agree on the step. Three defects caught before they did damage. Next week, the live filings, because that is now the only way to reach anything recent.

show.event: The Claude artifact page opens — 'Bulk Ingestion at Scale — week 2' in serif.
Five findings stagger in, one per spoken clause.

artifactLines: Scale: 14 quarters ingested. 80,571,213 holdings → 22,041,937 private → 5,806 marks, and every stage reconciles to the one above it.
Anthropic: 33 period ends, $11.79 → $333.60. A staircase, not a drift — a mark only moves when a funding round reprices it.
7 independent fund families agree at $259.14, to the cent, on the same date — 24 registrations, but 7 decision-makers.
The archive is keyed to FILING date and runs ~56 days late: 2026 Q2 stops at 30 Apr, so the $589 mark is unreachable in bulk.
Traps caught: Fidelity's VIP funds counted as 5 managers; SpaceX preferred priced exactly 10x common (309 of 624). Next: the live filings.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Take a fund you know, pull its last two Form N-PORT filings from EDGAR, and compare the period end date inside the filing with the date the filing was actually accepted. Then ask what that gap means for anything you would conclude from the latest data. That is the trap I walked into this week. Every dataset has a publication lag, and it is almost never the same as the label on the box.

show.event: Composer returns, greeting reads 'Your turn.' — the one greeting that drops the persona.
The suggested prompt types itself in as the narration reads it aloud, verbatim.
Running text reads 'paste this into Claude…'; the send button holds armed while the narration discusses what to look for.

props.command: Take a fund you know and pull its last two SEC Form N-PORT filings from EDGAR. Compare the period-end date INSIDE the filing with the date the filing was accepted. How far apart are they — and what does that gap mean for anything you'd conclude from "the latest data"?
